title: Passing a whole container, both ways

prereqs.why: One function takes the vector read-only by const reference, the other modifies it through a plain reference.
The container being passed around is a vector, and the functions use size() and indexing.
Three small functions, each with a signature that says what it is allowed to do.

statement:
Read `n` then `n` integers. Then write and use three functions:

```cpp
long long total(const std::vector<int>& v);   // reads, cannot modify
void addToAll(std::vector<int>& v, int d);    // modifies in place
void reverseIt(std::vector<int>& v);          // modifies in place
```

Print, in order:

```
total <sum of the original values>
after-add <the values with 7 added to each, space separated>
reversed <those values reversed, space separated>
total <sum again, which has changed>
```

```
input:   4
         1 2 3 4

output:  total 10
         after-add 8 9 10 11
         reversed 11 10 9 8
         total 38
```

The operations are applied in that order and each one builds on the last, so the
second `total` reflects both earlier changes.

### The point of the problem

Three signatures, three different contracts, and the contract is in the type:

| Signature | What the caller learns |
| --- | --- |
| `const std::vector<int>& v` | it will be read, not changed, and not copied |
| `std::vector<int>& v` | it will be changed in place |
| `std::vector<int> v` | a full copy is made, and changes are discarded |

The third is the one to avoid by accident. Passing a vector by value copies
every element, which for a large vector is real work done for nothing - and if
the function was supposed to modify it, nothing happens.

`const&` is the default for anything bigger than a machine word. It is cheap
like by-value for small types and free of copying for large ones, and the `const`
is a promise the compiler enforces: try to assign to `v` inside `total` and the
build fails.

### Boundary cases

`n = 0`: `total 0`, two empty lines, and `total 0` again. `n = 1`, where
reversing is a no-op. Negative values. Values whose sum does not fit in an
`int`, which is why `total` returns `long long`.

### Output format

Space separated, **no trailing space**; an empty vector prints the label and
nothing after it, so `after-add` on its own line.

### Platform assumptions

Each value fits in a 32-bit `int` and `n` is at most 1000, so the sum fits
comfortably in a 64-bit `long long` even at the extremes. `int` is assumed to be
at least 32 bits and `long long` at least 64, which the standard guarantees.
hints: `total` should accumulate into a `long long`, not an `int`: `long long s{}; for (int x : v) s += x;`. The addition widens because `s` is the wider type, so no intermediate overflow.
`addToAll` needs a by-reference range-for: `for (int& x : v) x += d;`. With `int x` it adds to a copy and the vector is untouched.

To reverse in place, swap from both ends: two indices walking inwards with `std::swap(v[i], v[j - 1])`. Or just call `std::reverse(v.begin(), v.end())` from `<algorithm>`, which is what you would write in real code.
